brief.topic: The Quiet Journey Inside a Ring

s01: A small circle sweeps out a ring.
How much space is inside that ring?
Its answer follows the journey of one point: the center of the circle.
First, look at the circular cross section.
Its area is pi times the small radius squared.
Its center travels around a larger circle.
That journey is two pi times the larger radius.
Multiply the area by that distance, and you get the volume.
But the inner side travels less than the outer side.
Why is the center allowed to speak for both?
Take two equally small pieces, equally far from the center.
One travels at radius R minus s.
The other travels at radius R plus s.
Their two journey lengths average to two pi R.
Pair up the little pieces across the whole disk.
Every pair has the same average journey.
As the pieces become tiny, each swept tube contributes its area times its journey.
Adding them gives the whole cross section times two pi R.
That is the volume of the ring.
This is an example of the centroid theorem of Pappus.
The rotation axis must stay outside the disk.
If the disk crosses the axis, swept parts overlap and this simple argument fails.
For our ordinary ring, the center quietly accounts for every little journey.
One circle, carried around another, becomes a volume.

scenes.narration:

First, look at the circular cross section. Its area is pi times the small radius squared. Its center travels around a larger circle. That journey is two pi times the larger radius. Multiply the area by that distance, and you get the volume.

But the inner side travels less than the outer side. Why is the center allowed to speak for both? Take two equally small pieces, equally far from the center. One travels at radius R minus s. The other travels at radius R plus s. Their two journey lengths average to two pi R.

Pair up the little pieces across the whole disk. Every pair has the same average journey. As the pieces become tiny, each swept tube contributes its area times its journey. Adding them gives the whole cross section times two pi R. That is the volume of the ring.

This is an example of the centroid theorem of Pappus. The rotation axis must stay outside the disk. If the disk crosses the axis, swept parts overlap and this simple argument fails. For our ordinary ring, the center quietly accounts for every little journey. One circle, carried around another, becomes a volume.
